title: How Makeup Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore the history and chemistry of makeup, from ancient Egyptian kohl and Sumerian lipstick through Elizabeth I's white lead face paint, the early 20th-century founding of cosmetics brands (Max Factor, Mabelline, Revlon, Estee Lauder), the 1950s lipstick wars, and how cosmetics are formulated. They then discuss US cosmetic safety regulation versus the EU approach, the proposed Personal Care Products Safety Act, the psychology and evolutionary theories of makeup, feminist views on makeup, men and makeup, and unusual cosmetic ingredients. The episode includes a sponsor/ad break, a listener mail segment about teaching English with the show in Shanghai, and a sign-off.

segments.title: Intro and International Women's Day banter
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about International Women's Day and wearing makeup, then introduce the topic of makeup and the roughly sixty billion dollar cosmetics industry.

segments.title: Ancient makeup: Sumer, Egypt, Greece and Rome
segments.summary: The etymology of cosmetics is discussed, and the hosts describe early makeup use in Sumer and Egypt, including kohl eye makeup made from copper, lead, ash and burnt almonds, which was believed to ward off the evil eye and deflect desert sunlight. Greek and Roman face painting with ground stones and minerals is also covered.

segments.title: Pale skin, cerussite, and Elizabeth I
segments.summary: Pre-medieval European women used pigments and hair curling, but pale skin later became fashionable as a sign of wealth, leading to lead-based whitening such as cerussite. The hosts discuss Elizabeth I's lead makeup and the myth that she went bald, with theories about hairline plucking and forehead status.

segments.title: Cosmetics founders and the rise of modern makeup
segments.summary: Many cosmetics brands were founded by named people, including Max Factor, Estee Lauder, and the Maybelline founder inspired by his sister Mabel. The hosts describe how modern makeup use grew with portraiture, affordable mirrors, photography, and the movies, where Max Factor created stage and film makeup such as foundation, eyeliner and lip products.

segments.title: Nail polish, Henry Ford, Revlon and the lipstick wars
segments.summary: Nail polish advanced in the 1920s after fast-drying lacquer research tied to Henry Ford's black Model T paint. Charles Revson of Revlon marketed matching nail polish and lipstick with Fire and Ice ads. Hazel Bishop's indelible lipstick sparked the lipstick wars, with Revlon's living lipstick trademark dispute and Revlon's sponsorship of The $64,000 Question ending the fight.

segments.title: Estee Lauder's department store sampling and the standard ingredients
segments.summary: Estee Lauder is credited with giving away free samples in department stores. The hosts note that by the 1950s and 1960s the cosmetics industry was established and that most makeup now uses largely the same basic ingredients.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Short break before the discussion of ingredients.

segments.title: How makeup is formulated
segments.summary: The hosts describe typical formulations: foundation with moisturizing base, filler, and iron oxide pigment; eyeliner with film formers, thickeners and pigments; eyeshadow with a base like talc or kaolin clay and a zinc or magnesium binder; and waterproof mascara.

segments.title: US cosmetic safety regulation vs the EU
segments.summary: The hosts explain that US cosmetic regulation has changed little since 1938, that the industry largely self-regulates, and that the EU presumes chemicals harmful until proven safe while the US presumes safety. They discuss parabens, phthalates, and the proposed Personal Care Products Safety Act introduced by Dianne Feinstein and Susan Collins, which would require adverse-effect reporting and periodic review of risky ingredients. They mention the Johnson and Johnson talc verdict and a critique by Jessica Assaf.

segments.title: Natural products, state law, and the psychology of makeup
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the lack of FDA definition for all natural claims, mineral makeup, California's Safe Cosmetics Act, and then turn to the psychology of beauty: symmetry, the golden ratio, sexual dimorphism, and the evolutionary theory that makeup signals fitness for mating.

segments.title: Feminism, men and makeup, and celebrity no-makeup movements
segments.summary: The hosts cover second-wave feminism's rejection of makeup, third-wave views on choice, historical male attempts to restrict makeup including an 1770 British annulment idea and a Roman poet's criticism, and the hashtag no makeup selfies campaign for cancer research. They also share personal anecdotes about makeup on set.

segments.title: Unusual cosmetic ingredients
segments.summary: The hosts briefly discuss unusual ingredients: tallow from animal fat including roadkill, a skincare product using cells from infant foreskin grown in a lab, snail slime extract, and lanolin from sheep's wool.

segments.title: Listener mail from Jason's Shanghai class
segments.summary: A listener named Jason, who teaches English at an international school in Shanghai, writes that students used the show for English practice and made their own podcasts. A clip of the student podcast is played.

segments.title: Outro and social media
segments.summary: The hosts close by inviting listeners to contact the show on Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website.
